study.title: Isaiah 65 - Judgment on the rebellion and promise of total renewal
study.overview: Isaiah 65 presents a strong contrast between a people who reject the voice of God and the servants who seek him. The chapter begins with the denunciation of Israel's idolatry and persistent disobedience, showing that the Lord responded with patience but also with justice. Then he promises to separate a faithful remnant, give him inheritance, new name and hope, and then extends the vision to new heavens and new earth, where joy, justice and peace encompass all creation.

outline.title: God lets themselves be found, but the people reject him
outline.explanation: The Lord declares that he showed himself to those who did not seek him, while his people remained rebellious, practicing forbidden cults and affronting his holiness. The divine answer is not silence, but just retribution to his works.

outline.title: Preservation of a remnant and promise of inheritance
outline.explanation: Even in judgment, God does not destroy everyone. He guards his servants, generates offspring for Jacob and Judah, and promises a place of rest and provision for the people who sought him.

outline.title: Separation between those who forsake the Lord and his servants
outline.explanation: Those who forget the holy mountain and surrender to lot and fate receive sword, famine, shame and curse. The servants of God receive contentment and a new name; the true God becomes the reference of his life and his oaths.

outline.title: New creation, full joy and peace in creation
outline.explanation: The Lord promises new heavens and new earth, with Jerusalem as a place of joy. There will be no more weeping, helplessness or useless work; God will answer even before the cry ends, and even the order of creation will be restored in peace on his holy mountain.

study.context: The chapter responds to an earlier prayer of lament and confession, showing that God had offered himself to his people, but they did not seek him. The text mentions idolatrous practices linked to cults in gardens, hills and hidden places, and this indicates a rooted religious infidelity. At the same time, the chapter broadens hope for a restoration horizon that some commentators relate to the call of the Gentiles and the new creation promised by God.
study.theology: The theology of the chapter unites justice and grace. God judges real sin, especially idolatry and refusal to hear his word, but does not abandon his redeeming purpose. He preserves a remnant, creates a people with a new identity and promises a cosmic renewal in which peace reaches even the animals. The final emphasis is not only on individual comfort, but on the complete transformation of reality under the holy rule of the Lord. The chapter also shows that true communion with God involves a response to his initiative: he makes himself, finds himself, calls, hears and restores.

scholarViews.insight: The Lord opened every opportunity for the people to seek them, but they did not; this highlights the persistent refusal of the people before the divine initiative.
The promise of new heavens and new earth points, in part, to an early restoration, but finds its full fulfillment in the gospel community and the final consummation.
The reference to the "jardins" shows pagan religion practices associated with fertility cults, which shows the idolatrous nature of the denounced rebellion.

questions: In which areas can I be resisting God's initiative, even listening to your voice clearly?
What practices or competing alleties today work, in practice, as "other altars" in the heart?
How should the promise of new heavens and new earth shape my expectations, my suffering and my decisions now?
study.practice: Read this chapter as a call to repentance and hope. Make an honest assessment of where you have followed your own thoughts instead of the word of God. Then pray asking the Lord to find you in your need, renew your joy in him and form in you habits consistent with the new people he is creating. At the same time, it sustains the hope that the righteousness of God does not end in the judgment: he also prepares a restored creation, where there will be no more harm or fear.
study.uncertainty: The text and the notes provided allow us to affirm the denunciation of idolatry, the preservation of a remnant and the hope of new creation; however, more specific historical details, dates of fulfillment and precise correlations with later events cannot be safely established only with these sources. In addition, the confessional readings of commentators on compliance in Israel, the Gentiles and the church should be understood as theological interpretations, not as indisputable conclusions of the text.
